Flag varieties, toric varieties, and suspensions:

Abstract.

We say that a group GG acts infinitely transitively on a set XX if for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} the induced diagonal action of GG is transitive on the cartesian mmth power Xm∖ΔX^{m}\setminus\Delta with the diagonals removed. We describe three classes of affine algebraic varieties such that their automorphism groups act infinitely transitively on their smooth loci. The first class consists of normal affine cones over flag varieties, the second of non-degenerate affine toric varieties, and the third of iterated suspensions over affine varieties with infinitely transitive automorphism groups of a reinforced type.

Key words and phrases:
Affine algebraic variety, automorphism, infinite transitivity, derivation

Introduction

All varieties in this paper are assumed being reduced and irreducible. Unless we explicitly precise a setting, the ground field 𝕜{\Bbbk} is supposed to be algebraically closed of characteristic zero.

An effective action of the additive group 𝔾a​(𝕜){\mathbb{G}}_{\rm a}({\Bbbk}) on an algebraic variety XX defines a one-parameter unipotent subgroup of the automorphism group Aut(X)\mathop{\rm Aut}(X). We let SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) denote the subgroup of Aut(X)\mathop{\rm Aut}(X) generated by all its one-parameter unipotent subgroups. In the sequel, we adopt the following definitions.

Definition 0.1.

Let XX be an algebraic variety over 𝕜{\Bbbk}. We say that a point x∈Xx\in X is flexible if the tangent space Tx​XT_{x}X is spanned by the tangent vectors to the orbits H.xH.x of one-parameter unipotent subgroups H⊆Aut(X)H\subseteq\mathop{\rm Aut}(X). The variety XX is called flexible if every smooth point x∈Xregx\in X_{\rm reg} is.

Definition 0.2.

An action of a group GG on a set AA is said to be mm-transitive if for every two tuples of pairwise distinct points (a1,a2,…,am)(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{m}) and (b1,b2,…,bm)(b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{m}) in AA there exists g∈Gg\in G such that g⁡(ai)=big(a_{i})=b_{i}, i=1,2,…,mi=1,2,\dots,m. The action which is mm-transitive for all m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} will be called infinitely transitive.

Clearly, for m>dimGm>\dim G the Lie group GG cannot act mm-transitively on a variety XX. In fact, due to the following theorem it cannot act even 44-transitively on a smooth simply connected variety.

Theorem 0.1.

(A. Borel [6, Théorèmes 5-6]) There exist no 33-transitive actions of a real Lie group GG on a simply connected non-compact variety, and such 22-transitive actions exist only on the Euclidean spaces ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} for n≥2n\geq 2. There exist no 44-transitive actions of GG on a compact simply connected variety, and such 33-transitive actions exist only on the spheres SnS^{n} for n≥2n\geq 2.

For a classification of 22- and 33-transitive Lie group actions see, e.g., [23] and [40]. See also [34] for the ”generic transitivity” of an action of an algebraic group GG, i. e. the existence of Zariski open orbits in the Cartesian powers of a given algebraic GG-variety.

The infinite transitivity of the full automorphism group is well known for the affine space 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} over 𝕜{\Bbbk}, where n≥2n\geq 2; see also [2] and [39] for the analytic counterpart and generalizations. This phenomenon takes place as well for any hypersurface XX in 𝔸n+1{\mathbb{A}}^{n+1} given by the equation u​v−f⁡(x1,…,xn−1)=0uv-f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})=0, where n≥3n\geq 3 and f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn−1]f\in{\Bbbk}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}] is a non-constant polynomial [21, §5]. In the sequel we call such a variety XX a suspension over Y=𝔸n−1Y={\mathbb{A}}^{n-1}. In the analytic category, similar phenomenons were studied in the spirit of the Andersen-Lempert-Varolin theory [2], [42], see, e.g., [12], [19], [38], and [41]. This concerns, in particular, the infinite transitivity on smooth affine algebraic varieties of certain subgroups of biholomorphic transformations generated by complete regular vector fields, see survey [20], especially §2(B) and Remark 2.2.

Following [21, §5], we are interested here in algebraic varieties XX such that the special automorphism group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts infinitely transitively on the smooth locus XregX_{\rm reg} of XX. We show, in particular, that this property is preserved when passing to a suspension.

Definition 0.3.

By a suspension over an affine variety YY we mean a hypersurface X⊆Y×𝔸2X\subseteq Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by the equation u​v−f⁡(y)=0uv-f(y)=0, where 𝔸2=Spec𝕜⁡[u,v]{\mathbb{A}}^{2}=\mathop{\rm Spec}{\Bbbk}[u,v] and f∈𝕜⁡[Y]f\in{\Bbbk}[Y] is non-constant. In particular, dimX=1+dimY\dim X=1+\dim Y.

Our main results can be formulated as follows. An affine variety is called non-degenerate if every invertible regular function on it is constant.

Theorem 0.2.
  1. (1)

    Consider a flag variety G/PG/P, where GG is a semisimple algebraic group, and PP is a parabolic subgroup in GG. Then every normal affine cone XX over G/PG/P is flexible and its special automorphism group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts infinitely transitively on the smooth locus XregX_{\rm reg}.

  2. (2)

    The analogous conclusion holds if XX is any non-degenerate affine toric variety of dimension at least 2.

  3. (3)

    Suppose that an affine variety XX is flexible and either X=𝔸1X={\mathbb{A}}^{1}, or dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2 and the special automorphism group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts infinitely transitively on the smooth locus XregX_{\rm reg}. Then all iterated suspensions over XX also have properties of flexibility and infinite transitivity of the special automorphism group.

Theorem 0.2(n) is proved in Section nn, where n=1,2,3n=1,2,3, respectively.

Smooth compact real algebraic surfaces with infinitely transitive automorphism groups were classified in [4], [5], [17], and [18]. In Theorem 3.3 we extend part 3 of Theorem 0.2 to real algebraic varieties, under certain additional restrictions. These restrictions were weakened in a recent paper [24]. In the particular case of a suspension over the affine line, the result remains valid over an arbitrary field of characteristic zero, see Theorem 3.1.

Recall [13, §9] that the Makar-Limanov invariant ML(X)\mathop{\rm ML}(X) of an affine variety XX is the intersection of the kernels of all locally nilpotent derivations of 𝕜⁡[X]{\Bbbk}[X], or, in other words, the subalgebra in 𝕜⁡[X]{\Bbbk}[X] of common invariants for all one-parameter unipotent subgroups of Aut(X)\mathop{\rm Aut}(X). From this definition it is straightforward that ML(X)=𝕜​[X]SAut(X)\mathop{\rm ML}(X)={\Bbbk}[X]^{\mathop{\rm SAut}(X)}. Hence the Makar-Limanov invariant of XX is trivial (that is ML(X)=𝕜\mathop{\rm ML}(X)={\Bbbk}) provided that the special automorphism group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts on XX with a dense open orbit (cf. [35]). In particular, this holds for the varieties in all the three classes from Theorem 0.2 (for the first two of them, see also [22, 3.16], [27], and [35]). On the other hand, ML(X)\mathop{\rm ML}(X) is trivial if XX is flexible. Indeed, if f∈𝕜​[X]SAut(X)f\in{\Bbbk}[X]^{\mathop{\rm SAut}(X)} then the differential d​fdf vanishes along the orbits of any unipotent subgroup, hence it vanishes on the tangent space at any flexible point of XregX_{\mathop{\rm reg}}. Since XX is flexible, ff is constant.

In the first preprint version of this paper we conjectured that for a variety of dimension at least 2 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero the transitivity of the group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) on XregX_{\rm reg}, the infinite transitivity of this group, and flexibility of XX are equivalent. Later on this conjecture was proved in [3]. Furthermore, in the same preprint version we proposed to characterize the class of affine varieties such that the group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts infinitely transitively on a Zariski open subset. This was also done in [3] (see Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 5.1) in terms of the field Makar-Limanov invariant FML(X)\mathop{\rm FML}(X), introduced by A. Liendo [28]. In [31], it is shown that affine cones over del Pezzo surfaces of degrees 4 and 5 are flexible, which implies infinite transitivity of the action of SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) on these varieties.

We are grateful to Dmitry Akhiezer, Shulim Kaliman, and Alvaro Liendo for useful discussions and references.

The next result provides part 1 of Theorem 0.2.

Theorem 1.1.

Let XX be the affine cone over a flag variety G/PG/P under an embedding G/P↪ℙNG/P\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{N} with projectively normal image. Then XX is flexible and the group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts mm-transitively on X\{0}X\backslash\{0\} for any m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}.

The flexibility follows from the next general observation.

Proposition 1.1.

If a semisimple linear algebraic group GG acts on an affine variety XX and this action is transitive on XregX_{\rm reg}, then XX is flexible.

Proof.

The group GG acts on XX with an open orbit Xreg=G.x0X_{\rm reg}=G.x_{0}. The dominant morphism onto this orbit φ:G→X\varphi:G\to X, g⟼g.x0g\longmapsto g.x_{0}, yields a surjection d​φ:𝔤→Tx0​Xd\varphi:{\mathfrak{g}}\to T_{x_{0}}X, where 𝔤=Lie⁡(G){\mathfrak{g}}={\rm Lie}(G). We claim that 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} is spanned by nilpotent elements over 𝕜{\Bbbk}, which implies the assertion. Indeed, consider the decomposition 𝔤=⨁i=1k𝔤i{\mathfrak{g}}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{k}{\mathfrak{g}}_{i} of 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} into simple ideals. Let 𝔥{\mathfrak{h}} be the span of the set of all nilpotent elements in 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}. This is an ad-submodule of 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} and so an ideal of 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}, hence a direct sum of some of the simple ideals 𝔤i{\mathfrak{g}}_{i}. However every simple ideal 𝔤i{\mathfrak{g}}_{i}, i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k, contains at least one nonzero nilpotent element. Therefore 𝔥=𝔤{\mathfrak{h}}={\mathfrak{g}}, as claimed. ∎

In the setting of Theorem 1.1, Xreg=XX_{\rm reg}=X if X≅𝔸nX\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{n} and Xreg=X∖{0}X_{\rm reg}=X\setminus\{0\} otherwise. Anyhow, the group GG acts transitively on X∖{0}X\setminus\{0\}, see, e.g., [36, Theorem 1]. Hence by Proposition 1.1 XX is flexible.

Let μ\mu be an extremal weight of the simple GG-module V⁡(λ)V(\lambda) different from λ\lambda. Lemma 1.1.

2. Automorphisms of affine toric varieties

As before, 𝕜{\Bbbk} stands for an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. In this section we consider an affine toric variety XX over 𝕜{\Bbbk} with a torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} acting effectively on XX. We assume that XX is non-degenerate, i.e., the only invertible regular functions on XX are constants or, which is equivalent, that X≇Y×𝔸∗1X\not\cong Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{*}, where 𝔸∗1=Spec𝕜⁡[t,t−1]≅𝔾m​(𝕜){\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{*}=\mathop{\rm Spec}{\Bbbk}[t,t^{-1}]\cong{\mathbb{G}}_{\rm m}({\Bbbk}).

The following result yields part 2 of Theorem 0.2.

Theorem 2.1.

Every non-degenerate affine toric variety XX of dimension n≥1n\geq 1 is flexible. If n≥2n\geq 2, for any m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} the group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts mm-transitively on the smooth locus XregX_{\mathop{\rm reg}} of XX.

We note that XX is flexible if Aut(X)\mathop{\rm Aut}(X) acts transitively on XregX_{\rm reg} and at least one smooth point is flexible on XX. Both of these properties will be established below. Let us first recall some necessary generalities on toric varieties.

Proposition 2.1.

Given a root e∈ℛ⁡(σ)e\in{\mathscr{R}}(\sigma). Let, as before, He⊆SAut(X)H_{e}\subseteq\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) be the associate one-parameter unipotent subgroup. Then the following holds.

    For every point x∈X∖XHex\in X\setminus X^{H_{e}}, the orbit He.xH_{e}.x meets exactly two 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbits 𝒪1{\mathscr{O}}_{1} and 𝒪2{\mathscr{O}}_{2} on XX, where dim𝒪1=1+dim𝒪2\dim{\mathscr{O}}_{1}=1+\dim{\mathscr{O}}_{2}.

  2. b)

    The intersection 𝒪2∩He.x{\mathscr{O}}_{2}\cap H_{e}.x consists of a single point, while

    𝒪1∩He.x=Re.y∀y∈𝒪1∩He.x.{\mathscr{O}}_{1}\cap H_{e}.x\ =\ R_{e}.y\qquad\forall y\in{\mathscr{O}}_{1}\cap H_{e}.x\,.
Proof.

a) The number of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbits in XX being finite, there exists a 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbit 𝒪1{\mathscr{O}}_{1} such that the intersection 𝒪1∩He.x{\mathscr{O}}_{1}\cap H_{e}.x is a Zariski open subset of He.xH_{e}.x. So He.x⊆𝒪1¯H_{e}.x\subseteq\overline{{\mathscr{O}}_{1}}. There is also another 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbit 𝒪2{\mathscr{O}}_{2} that meets He.xH_{e}.x. Indeed, otherwise He.x≅𝔸1H_{e}.x\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1} would be contained in a single 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbit 𝒪1{\mathscr{O}}_{1}. However, this is impossible because the regular invertible functions separate points on 𝒪1{\mathscr{O}}_{1}, and, consequently, either they do on He.xH_{e}.x. Since 𝒪2{\mathscr{O}}_{2} intersects 𝒪1¯\overline{{\mathscr{O}}_{1}}, we have 𝒪2⊆𝒪1¯{\mathscr{O}}_{2}\subseteq\overline{{\mathscr{O}}_{1}} and so dim𝒪2<dim𝒪1\dim{\mathscr{O}}_{2}<\dim{\mathscr{O}}_{1}.

We know that the torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} normalizes the unipotent subgroup HeH_{e}. Hence the elements of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} send the HeH_{e}-orbits into HeH_{e}-orbits. In particular, for every point q∈He.xq\in H_{e}.x the stabilizer 𝕋q{\mathbb{T}}_{q} preserves the orbit He.xH_{e}.x. For all q∈𝒪1∩He.xq\in{\mathscr{O}}_{1}\cap H_{e}.x the stabilizer is the same. Since He.x⊆𝒪1¯=X𝕋qH_{e}.x\subseteq\overline{{\mathscr{O}}_{1}}=X^{{\mathbb{T}}_{q}}, this stabilizer acts trivially on He.xH_{e}.x. Thus 𝕋r⊇𝕋q{\mathbb{T}}_{r}\supseteq{\mathbb{T}}_{q} for any point r∈He.xr\in H_{e}.x, and 𝕋r=𝕋q{\mathbb{T}}_{r}={\mathbb{T}}_{q} if and only if r∈𝒪1∩He.xr\in{\mathscr{O}}_{1}\cap H_{e}.x.

Fix a point p∈𝒪2∩He.xp\in{\mathscr{O}}_{2}\cap H_{e}.x. Let (𝒪1,𝒪2)({\mathscr{O}}_{1},{\mathscr{O}}_{2}) be a pair of 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}-orbits on XX with 𝒪2⊆𝒪1¯{\mathscr{O}}_{2}\subseteq\overline{{\mathscr{O}}_{1}}, where 𝒪i=𝒪σi⊥{\mathscr{O}}_{i}={\mathscr{O}}_{\sigma_{i}^{\bot}} for a face σi\sigma_{i} of the cone σ\sigma, i=1,2i=1,2.     Suppose that the points Qj1,…,QjlQ_{j_{1}},\ldots,Q_{j_{l}} belong to the same RsR_{s}-orbit 𝒯(s){\mathscr{T}}^{(s)}. Then their images under a general shift on the line 𝒯(s)¯≅𝔸1\overline{{\mathscr{T}}^{(s)}}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1} belong to distinct RrR_{r}-orbits for every r≠sr\neq s.

Proof.

a) Given a κ\kappath root of unity ε\varepsilon, the linear equation

ti+a=ε⁡(tj+a)t_{i}+a=\varepsilon(t_{j}+a)

is satisfied for at most one value of aa. It implies a).

The assertion of b) holds since the RsR_{s}-action on XX, lifted via (2.10), affects only the component ti,st_{i,s} of the point QiQ_{i} in (2.11), while the Θ\Theta-action on 𝔾m​(𝕜)n{\mathbb{G}}_{\rm m}({\Bbbk})^{n} replaces the component ti,rt_{i,r} (r≠sr\neq s) by a κ\kappa-equivalent one.

Now c) follows immediately from a) and b). Indeed, for i≠ji\neq j the intersection of any RiR_{i}- and RjR_{j}-orbits is at most finite. ∎

Lemma 2.8.

In the notation as above there exists ψ∈SAut(X)\psi\in\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) such that the points ψ⁡(Q1),…,ψ⁡(Qm)\psi(Q_{1}),\ldots,\psi(Q_{m}) belong to different R1R_{1}-orbits in 𝕋.x0{\mathbb{T}}.x_{0}.

Proof.

By our assumption n≥2n\geq 2, so there is an R2R_{2}-action on XX. Let 𝒯0(2),…,𝒯k(2){\mathscr{T}}_{0}^{(2)},\ldots,{\mathscr{T}}_{k}^{(2)} be the distinct R2R_{2}-orbits passing through the points Q1,…,QmQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{m} so that this collection splits into k+1k+1 disjoint pieces. We may assume that the piece on 𝒯0(2){\mathscr{T}}_{0}^{(2)} is Q1,…,QlQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{l}. Applying Lemma 2.6 to ρe=ρ2\rho_{e}=\rho_{2}, we find a one-parameter unipotent subgroup H⊆Stab𝒯1(2),…,𝒯k(2)(𝒯0(2))H\subseteq\mathop{\rm Stab}_{{\mathscr{T}}_{1}^{(2)},\ldots,{\mathscr{T}}_{k}^{(2)}}({\mathscr{T}}_{0}^{(2)}) acting by shifts on 𝒯0(2)¯≅𝔸1\overline{{\mathscr{T}}_{0}^{(2)}}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. By Lemma 2.7 the images of Q1,…,QlQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{l} under a general shift lie in different RrR_{r}-orbits for every r≠2r\neq 2, while all the other points QjQ_{j}, j>lj>l, remain fixed. Applying the same procedure subsequently to the other pieces, we finally obtain an automorphism ψ∈SAut(X)\psi\in\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) such that the points ψ⁡(Q1),…,ψ⁡(Qm)\psi(Q_{1}),\ldots,\psi(Q_{m}) belong to different RrR_{r}-orbits for every r≠2r\neq 2. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.1. Let us start with the infinite transitivity. By virtue of Lemma 2.8 we may assume that the orbits 𝒯j(1)=R1.Qj{\mathscr{T}}_{j}^{(1)}=R_{1}.Q_{j}, j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m, are all distinct. By Lemma 2.6 we can change the component t1,jt_{1,j} of a point QjQ_{j} arbitrarily while fixing the other components and as well the other points of our collection. Thus we can achieve that t1,j=jt_{1,j}=j for all j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m. This guarantees that for any l≥2l\geq 2 the orbits Rl.Q1,…,Rl.QmR_{l}.Q_{1},\ldots,R_{l}.Q_{m} are pairwise distinct. Applying Lemma 2.6 again to every RlR_{l}-orbit for l=2,…,nl=2,\ldots,n, we can reach the standard collection Q1(0),…,Qm(0)Q^{(0)}_{1},\ldots,Q_{m}^{(0)} as in (2.13) with tl,j=jt_{l,j}=j for all j=1,…,m,l=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,m,\,\,l=1,\ldots,n. This proves the infinite transitivity statement in Theorem 2.1.

The proof of flexibility is in the next lemma.

Lemma 2.9.

Every non-degenerate affine toric variety XX is flexible.

Proof.

If dimX=1\dim X=1, then X≅𝔸1X\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, and the assertion is evidently true. Further we suppose that dimX≥2\dim X\geq 2. We already know that the group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts (infinitely) transitively on XregX_{\mathop{\rm reg}}. Hence it is enough to find just one flexible point on XregX_{\mathop{\rm reg}}. The stabilizer Stab(x0)⊆𝔾m​(𝕜)n\mathop{\rm Stab}(x_{0})\subseteq{\mathbb{G}}_{\rm m}({\Bbbk})^{n} being finite, the tangent map Tg​𝔾m​(𝕜)n→Tx0​XT_{g}{\mathbb{G}}_{\rm m}({\Bbbk})^{n}\to T_{x_{0}}X is surjective at each point g∈Stab(x0)g\in\mathop{\rm Stab}(x_{0}). Hence the tangent vectors at x0x_{0} to the orbits Ri.x0R_{i}.x_{0}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, span the tangent space Tx0​XT_{x_{0}}X. By Remark 2.1, for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n there exists a root ei∈ℛ⁡(σ)e_{i}\in{\mathscr{R}}(\sigma) such that ρi=ρei\rho_{i}=\rho_{e_{i}}. Example 2.2.

Consider a singular affine toric surface Xd,e=𝔸2/GdX_{d,e}={\mathbb{A}}^{2}/G_{d}, where dd and ee are coprime integers with 0<e<d0<e<d, and GdG_{d} is the cyclic group generated by a primitive ddth root of unity ζ\zeta, which acts on the plane 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} via ζ.(x,y)=(ζ​x,ζe​y)\zeta.(x,y)=(\zeta x,\zeta^{e}y). It is well known (see [11], [15], and [32]) that for e≥2e\geq 2 the smooth locus (Xd,e)reg=Xd,e∖{0}(X_{d,e})_{\mathop{\rm reg}}=X_{d,e}\setminus\{0\} is not isomorphic to a homogeneous space of any affine algebraic group. However Xd,e∖{0}X_{d,e}\setminus\{0\} is homogeneous under the action of the infinite dimensional group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X).

3. Affine suspensions

In this section we prove part 3 of Theorem 0.2. Let us first recall some necessary notions.

Definition 3.1.

Let X(0)X^{(0)} be an affine variety. By a cylinder over X(0)X^{(0)} we mean the product X(0)×𝔸1X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. Given a nonconstant regular function f1∈𝕜⁡[X(0)]f_{1}\in{\Bbbk}[X^{(0)}], we define a new affine variety

X(1)=Susp(X(0),f1):={f1(x)−uv=0}⊆X(0)×𝔸2,X^{(1)}=\mathop{\rm Susp}(X^{(0)},f_{1}):=\{f_{1}(x)-uv=0\}\subseteq X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2},

called a suspension over X(0)X^{(0)}. By recursion, for any l∈ℕl\in{\mathbb{N}} we obtain the iterated suspension X(l)=Susp(X(l−1),fl)X^{(l)}=\mathop{\rm Susp}(X^{(l-1)},f_{l}).

For instance, starting with X(0)=𝔸kX^{(0)}={\mathbb{A}}^{k}, we arrive at the llth suspension X(l)X^{(l)} given in the affine space

𝔸k+2​l=Spec𝕜⁡[x1,…,xk,u1,v1,…,ul,vl]{\mathbb{A}}^{k+2l}=\mathop{\rm Spec}{\Bbbk}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},u_{1},v_{1},\ldots,u_{l},v_{l}]

by the system of equations

(3.1) {u1​v1−f1​(x1,x2,…,xk)=0u2​v2−f2​(x1,x2,…,xk,u1,v1)=0…ul​vl−fl​(x1,x2,…,xk,u1,v1,u2,v2,…,ul−1,vl−1)=0,\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{1}v_{1}&-f_{1}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k})=0\\ u_{2}v_{2}&-f_{2}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k},u_{1},v_{1})=0\\ &\ldots\\ u_{l}v_{l}&-f_{l}(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k},u_{1},v_{1},u_{2},v_{2},\dots,u_{l-1},v_{l-1})=0,\\ \end{aligned}\right.

where for every i=1,2,…,li=1,2,\ldots,l the polynomial fi∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xk,u1,v1,…,ui−1,vi−1]f_{i}\in{\Bbbk}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},u_{1},v_{1},\ldots,u_{i-1},v_{i-1}] is non-constant modulo the ideal (u1​v1−f1,…,ui−1​vi−1−fi−1)(u_{1}v_{1}-f_{1},\ldots,u_{i-1}v_{i-1}-f_{i-1}).

We prove part 3 of Theorem 0.2 separately for suspensions over a line and over a variety of dimension at least 2. For suspensions over a line, the assertion remains true over an arbitrary field of characteristic zero, under an additional restriction on the function f=f1f=f_{1}.

Theorem 3.1.

Let 𝕜{\Bbbk} be a field of characteristic zero and let f∈𝕜⁡[x]f\in{\Bbbk}[x] be a polynomial such that f⁡(𝕜)=𝕜f({\Bbbk})={\Bbbk}. Consider a surface X⊆𝔸𝕜3X\subseteq{\mathbb{A}}_{\Bbbk}^{3} given by the equation f⁡(x)−u​v=0.f(x)-uv=0\,. Then XX is flexible and the special automorphism group SAut(X)\mathop{\rm SAut}(X) acts mm-transitively on XregX_{\mathop{\rm reg}} for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}.

In higher dimensions, part 3 of Theorem 0.2 can be restated as follows.

Theorem 3.2.

Let 𝕜{\Bbbk} be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let X(0)X^{(0)} be a flexible affine variety. Assume that either X(0)≅𝔸1X^{(0)}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, or dimX(0)⩾2\dim X^{(0)}\geqslant 2 and the special automorphism group SAut(X(0))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(0)}) acts mm-transitively on Xreg(0)X^{(0)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. Then every iterated suspension X(l)X^{(l)} over X(0)X^{(0)}, l≥1l\geq 1, is flexible and the special automorphism group SAut(X(l))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(l)}) acts mm-transitively on Xreg(l)X^{(l)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}.

Since the assumptions of the theorem are fulfilled for the affine space X(0)=𝔸kX^{(0)}={\mathbb{A}}^{k}, k≥1k\geq 1, we can conclude that for every k,l≥1k,l\geq 1 the affine variety X(l)⊆𝔸k+2​lX^{(l)}\subseteq{\mathbb{A}}^{k+2l} defined by (3.1) is flexible, and the group SAut(X(l))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(l)}) acts infinitely transitively on Xreg(l)X^{(l)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}}.

The proof of Theorem 3.2, with minor changes, works also for real algebraic varieties and leads to the following result.

Theorem 3.3.

Let X(0)X^{(0)} be a flexible real affine algebraic variety. Suppose that the smooth locus Xreg(0)X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)} is connected and the special automorphism group SAut(X(0))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(0)}) acts mm-transitively on Xreg(0)X^{(0)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. Consider the iterated suspensions X(i)=Susp(X(i−1),fi)X^{(i)}=\mathop{\rm Susp}(X^{(i-1)},f_{i}), where the functions fi∈ℝ⁡[X(i−1)]f_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}[X^{(i-1)}] satisfy the conditions fi​(Xreg(i−1))=ℝf_{i}(X^{(i-1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}})={\mathbb{R}}, i=1,…,li=1,\ldots,l. Then for every i=1,…,li=1,\ldots,l the variety X(i)X^{(i)} is flexible and the special automorphism group SAut(X(i))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(i)}) acts mm-transitively on Xreg(i)X^{(i)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}.

The infinite transitivity in Theorems 3.1–3.3 is proved in Subsections 3.1–3.3, respectively. The flexibility in all the three cases is established in Subsection 3.4.

3.1. Suspensions over a line

3.2. Infinite transitivity in higher dimensions

Lemma 3.1.

Lemma 3.2.

attains its maximal value s−dimX(0)s-\dim X^{(0)} at PP. The corresponding matrix for X(1)X^{(1)} is

Remark 3.1.

Let AA be an affine algebra. Recall (see [21]) that an affine modification of AA with center (I,v)(I,v), where I⊆AI\subseteq A is an ideal and v∈Iv\in I is not a zero divisor, is the quotient algebra A⁡[I​t]/(1−v​t)A[It]/(1-vt), where

A⁡[I​t]=A⊕⨁n=1∞(I​t)n≅A⊕I⊕I2⊕…=BlI​(A)A[It]=A\oplus\bigoplus_{n=1}^{\infty}(It)^{n}\cong A\oplus I\oplus I^{2}\oplus\ldots={\rm Bl}_{I}(A)

is the Rees algebra of the pair (A,I)(A,I), and tt is a formal symbol.

Geometrically, the variety Spec(A⁡[I​t]/(1−v​t))\mathop{\rm Spec}\,(A[It]/(1-vt)) can be obtained from X=SpecAX=\mathop{\rm Spec}A as follows. First we perform a blowup of XX with the center II, and then remove the proper transform of the zero divisor V⁡(v)V(v) in XX from BlI​(X){\rm Bl}_{I}(X), which results again in an affine variety. (We note that this proper transform meets the exceptional divisor EE, since v∈Iv\in I; see [21, §1] for more details).

According to [21, Example 1.4 and §5], the suspension X(1)=Susp(X(0),f)X^{(1)}=\mathop{\rm Susp}(X^{(0)},f) can be viewed as an affine modification of X(0)×𝔸1X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} (where 𝔸1=Spec𝕜⁡[v]{\mathbb{A}}^{1}=\mathop{\rm Spec}{\Bbbk}[v]) with the center (I1=(v,f),v)(I_{1}=(v,f),v) along the divisor v=0v=0. Interchanging vv and uu, we may also regard the variety X(1)X^{(1)} as an affine modification of the product X(0)×𝔸1X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, where this time 𝔸1=Spec𝕜⁡[u]{\mathbb{A}}^{1}=\mathop{\rm Spec}{\Bbbk}[u], with the center (I2=(u,f),u)(I_{2}=(u,f),u) along the divisor u=0u=0. The exceptional divisors of these two modifications (v=0v=0 and u=0u=0, respectively) are both isomorphic to X(0)×𝔸1X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} but different as subvarieties of X(1)X^{(1)}. For every c∈𝕜c\in{\Bbbk} we denote by Uc={u=c}U_{c}=\{u=c\} and Vc={v=c}V_{c}=\{v=c\} the level hypersurfaces in X(1)X^{(1)}, which are widely used in the sequel.

In [21, §2] there was developed a method which allows to extend an LND ∂\partial to the affine modification provided that ∂\partial stabilizes the center of the modification. In Lemma 3.3 (see below) we concretize this method in our particular case of affine suspensions.

Given an LND δ0\delta_{0} of an affine domain A0A_{0} and a polynomial q∈𝕜⁡[z]q\in{\Bbbk}[z] with q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0, we can define a new LND δ′=δ′​(δ0,q)\delta^{\prime}=\delta^{\prime}(\delta_{0},q) on A′=A0⊗𝕜⁡[v]A^{\prime}=A_{0}\otimes{\Bbbk}[v], where vv is a new variable, as follows. Suppose that A0A_{0} is generated by x1,x2,…,xsx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{s}. Then δ′\delta^{\prime} is given in coordinates by

(3.4) δ′(xi)=q(v)δ0(xi),i=1,2,…,s,δ′(v)=0.\delta^{\prime}(x_{i})=q(v)\delta_{0}(x_{i}),\quad i=1,2,\ldots,s,\qquad\delta^{\prime}(v)=0.

3.3. Suspensions over real varieties

Here we prove Theorem 3.3. We need the following elementary lemma.

Lemma 3.6.

Let YY be a smooth connected real manifold of dimension at least 2. Then for any continuous function f:Y→ℝf:Y\to{\mathbb{R}} the level set f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) is infinite for each c∈Intf⁡(Y)c\in\mathop{\rm Int}f(Y).

Proof.

Under our assumptions Intf⁡(Y)⊆ℝ\mathop{\rm Int}f(Y)\subseteq{\mathbb{R}} is an open interval. Choose two points y1,y2∈Yy_{1},y_{2}\in Y such that f⁡(y1)=c1<cf(y_{1})=c_{1}<c and f⁡(y2)=c2>cf(y_{2})=c_{2}>c. We can join them by a smooth path ll in YY. There exists a tubular neighborhood UU of ll diffeomorphic to a cylinder Δ×I\Delta\times I, where I=[0,1]I=[0,1] and Δ\Delta is a ball of dimension dimΔ=dimY−1≥1\dim\Delta=\dim Y-1\geq 1. So there exists a continuous family of paths joining y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} within UU such that any two of them meet only at their ends y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}. Since the hypersurface f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) separates YY, each of these paths crosses it. In particular, f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) is infinite. ∎

The proof of Theorem 3.3 differs just slightly from that of Theorem 3.2. Hence it is enough to indicate the necessary changes.

Sketch of the proof of Theorem 3.3. The assumption that the field 𝕜{\Bbbk} is algebraically closed was actually used in the proof of Theorem 3.2 only on two occasions. Namely, in the proofs of Lemma 3.5 and of the infinite transitivity in Theorem 3.2 we exploited the fact that under our assumptions the level sets (Vck∩Xreg(1))∖U0(V_{c_{k}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}})\setminus U_{0} and U1∩Vci∩Xreg(1)U_{1}\cap V_{c_{i}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} are of positive dimension, hence are infinite. For 𝕜=𝕜¯{\Bbbk}=\overline{{\Bbbk}} the latter follows from the Krull theorem and the dimension count. In the case where 𝕜=ℝ{\Bbbk}={\mathbb{R}}, we can deduce the same conclusion using Lemma 3.6. Indeed, in the notation as above, for every ci≠0c_{i}\neq 0 the restrictions

π:Vci∩Xreg(1)=(Vci)reg→Xreg(0),π:U1∩Vci∩Xreg(1)→f−1​(ci)∩Xreg(0)\pi\colon V_{c_{i}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}}=(V_{c_{i}})_{\mathop{\rm reg}}\to X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)},\qquad\pi\colon U_{1}\cap V_{c_{i}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}}\to f^{-1}(c_{i})\cap X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)}

are isomorphisms. Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.3 the smooth real manifold Xreg(0)X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)} has dimension ≥2\geq 2 and is connected. Since f⁡(Xreg(0))=ℝf(X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)})={\mathbb{R}}, by Lemma 3.6 the level set f−1​(ci)∩Xreg(0)f^{-1}(c_{i})\cap X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)} is infinite. Since ck≠0c_{k}\neq 0, the set (Vck∩Xreg(1))∖U0⊇U1∩Vck∩Xreg(1)(V_{c_{k}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}})\setminus U_{0}\supseteq U_{1}\cap V_{c_{k}}\cap X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} is infinite too.

A posteriori, the manifold Xreg(1)X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} is also connected. Hence by recursion we can apply the argument to the iterated suspensions X(i)X^{(i)} over X(0)X^{(0)}, i=1,…,li=1,\ldots,l.

3.4. Flexibility

To complete the proofs of Theorems 3.1–3.3, it remains to establish the flexibility of X(1)X^{(1)}.

Lemma 3.7.

Under the assumptions of any one of Theorems 3.1–3.3 the variety X(1)X^{(1)} is flexible.

Proof.

We already know that the group SAut(X(1))\mathop{\rm SAut}(X^{(1)}) acts transitively on Xreg(1)X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(1)}. Hence, similarly as in the proof of Lemma 2.9, it suffices to find just one flexible point P′=(P,u,v)∈Xreg(1)P^{\prime}=(P,u,v)\in X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(1)}.

The function f∈𝕜⁡[X(0)]f\in{\Bbbk}[X^{(0)}] being non-constant, d​f​(P)≠0df(P)\neq 0 at some point P∈Xreg(0)P\in X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(0)} with f⁡(P)≠0f(P)\neq 0. Due to our assumption X(0)X^{(0)} is flexible. Hence there exist nn locally nilpotent derivations ∂0(1),…,∂0(n)∈Der𝕜[X(0)]\partial_{0}^{(1)},\ldots,\partial_{0}^{(n)}\in\mathop{\rm Der}{\Bbbk}[X^{(0)}], where n=dimX(0)n=\dim X^{(0)}, such that the corresponding vector fields ξ1,…,ξn\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n} span the tangent space TP​X(0)T_{P}X^{(0)}, i.e.,

rk(ξ1​(P)…ξn​(P))=n.\mathop{\rm rk}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\xi_{1}(P)\\ \ldots\\ \xi_{n}(P)\\ \end{array}\right)=n\,.

It follows that ∂0(i)(f)​(P)≠0\partial_{0}^{(i)}(f)(P)\neq 0 for some index i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.

Let now P′=(P,u0,v0)∈Xreg(1)P^{\prime}=(P,u_{0},v_{0})\in X_{\mathop{\rm reg}}^{(1)} be a point such that π⁡(P′)=P\pi(P^{\prime})=P. Since u0​v0=f⁡(P)≠0u_{0}v_{0}=f(P)\neq 0, the point P′P^{\prime} is hyperbolic. Letting q⁡(v)=vq(v)=v in Lemma 3.3 we obtain nn LNDs

∂1(1),…,∂1(n)∈Der𝕜[X(1)], where∂1(j)=∂1(j)(∂0(j),v).\partial_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,\partial_{1}^{(n)}\in\mathop{\rm Der}{\Bbbk}[X^{(1)}],\quad\mbox{ where}\quad\partial_{1}^{(j)}=\partial_{1}^{(j)}(\partial_{0}^{(j)},v)\,.

Interchanging uu and vv and letting j=ij=i, we get yet another LND

∂2(i)=∂2(i)(∂0(i),u)∈Der𝕜[X(1)].\partial_{2}^{(i)}=\partial_{2}^{(i)}(\partial_{0}^{(i)},u)\in\mathop{\rm Der}{\Bbbk}[X^{(1)}]\,.

Let us show that the corresponding n+1n+1 vector fields span the tangent space TP′​X(1)T_{P^{\prime}}X^{(1)} at P′P^{\prime}, as required. We can view ∂1(1),…,∂1(n),∂2(i)\partial_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,\partial_{1}^{(n)},\partial_{2}^{(i)} as LNDs in Der𝕜​[X(0)]​[u,v]\mathop{\rm Der}{\Bbbk}[X^{(0)}][u,v] preserving the ideal (u​v−f)(uv-f), which means that the corresponding vector fields are tangent to the hypersurface

X(1)={uv−f(P)=0}⊆X(0)×𝔸2.X^{(1)}=\{uv-f(P)=0\}\subseteq X^{(0)}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\,.

The values of these vector fields at P′∈Xreg(1)P^{\prime}\in X^{(1)}_{\mathop{\rm reg}} yield an (n+1)×(n+2)(n+1)\times(n+2)-matrix

E=(v0​ξ1​(P)∂0(1)(f)​(P)0...v0​ξn​(P)∂0(n)(f)​(P)0u0​ξi​(P)0∂0(i)(f)​(P)).E=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}v_{0}\xi_{1}(P)&\partial_{0}^{(1)}(f)(P)&0\\ \leaders{\hbox{.}}{\hfill}&\leaders{\hbox{.}}{\hfill}&\leaders{\hbox{.}}{\hfill}\\ v_{0}\xi_{n}(P)&\partial_{0}^{(n)}(f)(P)&0\\ u_{0}\xi_{i}(P)&0&\partial_{0}^{(i)}(f)(P)\\ \end{array}\right)\,.

The first nn rows of EE are linearly independent, and the last one is independent from the preceding ones since ∂0(i)(f)​(P)≠0\partial_{0}^{(i)}(f)(P)\neq 0.
